item.title: [Heavy.com] Red Sox Trade Pitch Lands Elly De La Cruz For Wilyer Abreu-Led 4-Player Haul
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Vankin

item.content:encoded:
In a new trade pitch published Wednesday and aimed at the Boston Red Sox, Elly De La Cruz would bring his 30-homer, 30-steal power and speed to Fenway Park, but the cost would be slugging right fielder Wilyer Abreu, top prospect Franklin Arias and two more players headed to the Cincinnati Reds.
That is the swap proposed by Red Sox podcaster Robbie Hyde, and posted to Baseball Trade Values Wednesday. Cincinnati would also receive infielder Kristian Campbell and backup catcher-first baseman Mickey Gasper. The site’s valuation model scores that four-player package at 68.1 against 66.4 for De La Cruz.
Would Hyde’s trade pitch solve the Red Sox offensive production problem that ultimately led to their quick elimination by the New York Yankees in the American League wild-card series, when Boston managed only two runs in 18 innings?
Let’s examine the deal.
Elly De La Cruz Trade Package for Boston Red Sox
De La Cruz, a 24-year-old switch-hitting shortstop born in Sabana Grande de Boya, Dominican Republic, stands 6-foot-6 and debuted June 6, 2023, against the Dodgers. The two-time All-Star hit .283/.365/.515 with 30 home runs, 30 stolen bases and 5.6 WAR this season, according to Baseball-Reference‘s player page. His career line: .262/.338/.463, 90 homers and 169 steals in 563 games. He earns $800,000, according to Spotrac‘s contract tracker, reaches arbitration in 2027 and hits free agency in 2030.
Abreu, 27, a left-handed right fielder born in Maracaibo, Venezuela, owns Gold Gloves from 2024 and 2025, and is likely in line for another one this year. He hit .248/.327/.446 with 24 homers and a league-best 38 doubles in 2026. His career totals stand at .253/.327/.457, 63 homers, 13.5 WAR in 432 games.
Arias, a 20-year-old shortstop from Caracas, Venezuela, signed with Boston in January 2023. He hit .323 with 25 homers, 91 RBI and a .957 OPS across Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester. Prospect evaluators rank Arias as Boston’s No. 1 prospect, and No. 3 in baseball overall.
Campbell, 24, a Chattanooga, Tennessee, native and 2023 fourth-round pick, signed an eight-year, $60 million extension in April 2025 after a sizzling MLB debut that month. But he quickly slumped and was demoted. He hit .320/.440/.524 with six homers at Worcester after July 1, according to RotoWire. The Baseball Trade Values model values his production at 33.4 against 55 in remaining salary, a surplus of -21.6.
Gasper, 30, a Merrimack, New Hampshire, native out of Bryant and a 27th-round Yankees pick in 2018, returned to Boston on a February waiver claim. He hit .251/.357/.466 with 10 homers in 191 at-bats, including an eye-popping 1.671 OPS in August, according to MLB.com.

Boston Red Sox Power Problem After Wilyer Abreu Exit
De La Cruz out-homered Abreu 30 to 24 and out-slugged him by 69 points. His 94.7 mph average exit velocity and 54.9% hard-hit rate also top Abreu’s 89.8 mph and 43.6%.
Then comes the other column. Abreu produced 5.9 WAR to De La Cruz’s 5.6, because his right-field defense rated +28 runs this season (+60 for his career) while De La Cruz rated -7 at shortstop. Abreu already posted a 117 OPS+, so the swap converts one productive regular into a 142 OPS+ hitter and opens a vacancy in right field.
Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow has identified the lineup as an area for supplements.
“We obviously have a lot of work to do,” Breslow said at the Red Sox’ season-ending news conference, as quoted by Tim Healey of The Boston Globe.
The money runs two directions. Boston sheds Campbell’s $60 million deal, the only negative-value contract in the model’s ledger. Cincinnati’s side shows De La Cruz’s remaining control at 192.1 in production against 125.8 in salary, while Abreu checks in at 71.1 against 46.9.
Arias alone rates 63.6, within 2.8 points of De La Cruz. Cincinnati would receive him, a Gold Glove outfielder and Campbell’s contract, and would give up one star.
Boston gets the bigger bat. Cincinnati gets the bigger return. Who says no?

item.content:encoded:
The Wild Card series against the Yankees was probably the worst way for the 2026 season to end. Everything that was a problem at any point - struggles to score runs, the bullpen, injuries - all happened at the same time and within a matter of minutes. Two games in a row ended the Red Sox season. This wasn’t the plan. As all the Sox players returned from the WBC to Fort Myers, many riding hot streaks, this looked like a team ready to rocket. Yes, there were questions entering the season. But there were answers that hadn’t been fully formed yet.
After the 2025 season, the Sox were desperate for infield help. Trevor Story, not a guarantee of health or success himself, since arriving in Boston, was coming off a tremendous year, his best for the Red Sox. The rest of the infield was a question mark. Third base was more-or-less vacant after Alex Bregman opted out. Second base was going to be a battle with the future potential of Marcelo Mayer as a leading contestant. First base? Triston Casas? Maybe? Catcher, using the more generous definition of infield, was a tandem based on Carlos Narváez hitting in 2025 and Connor Wong, who couldn’t hit at all. There were at least two guys, which was more than could be said about first base.
Craig Breslow looked at the free agent market. He looked at the trade market. He looked at his own farm system. And in two phases he built the roster that he would live or die with.
We know about phase one. Caleb Durbin was acquired from the Milwaukee Brewers. Willson Contreras was acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals. Isaiah Kiner-Falefa was signed to platoon (kinda) with Mayer.
On the free agent market, the Red Sox went in the opposite direction. The promise/hope was two bats. And they passed on Pete Alonso, Alex Bregman, Bo Bichette etc. Aside from Contreras there were no big bats.
What Durbin would share with Willson, besides become Mini Bowser to his Bowser, was control. Contreras was guaranteed to be in town through 2027 with an option for 2028. Durbin will not hit free agency until the 2030s. The same with Mayer. Ranger Suarez, on the other side of the ball, also was signed long-term.
As it would turn out Willson Contreras would not even sniff competition from Triston Casas, who would face a series of injuries that would cost him the season. Not that anyone was worried about having too many first basemen. Caleb Durbin would start off slow with the bat, glacial even, but provide solid defense. He’d go on to set a new career high in home runs while, likely, competing for a Gold Glove.
Marcelo Mayer would underperform and then get hurt. Carlos Narváez would revert to his reputation as a bat-second player. While Connor Wong would provide some offense in a bounce-back season, the catcher tandem as a whole was underwater.
Phase two would be at the deadline. With Durbin rounding into form as The Durbinator, Breslow and his team set their sights on second base and catcher. Turning Connelly Early into Curtis Mead gave them another second baseman with control for years to come. And while the sample size is small, Mead hit 17 home runs in just 87 games. Adding a 30-homer threat to second base would be a tremendous pillar of the offense. Mayer would be traded separately, Mead would get hurt, but the plan was in place.
Similarly, the massive all-in prospect trade for Adley Rutschman was for 2026 and 2027. Connor Wong isn’t a free agent until after the 2028 season so catcher is set for another year and they have time to evaluate Rutschman or find a replacement before 2028. For Breslow’s plan through this summer, when he didn’t know he’d be extended, that’s all that mattered. Build then best team for what could be his last season if they struggled.
Entering 2027 the Red Sox have two catchers. They have an entire starting infield, plus top prospect Franklin Arias. They have Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Wilyer Abreu (plus control of Jarren Duran, and Masataka Yoshida, and Kristian Campbell) in the outfield.
The rotation has Payton Tolle, Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, and Jake Bennett. Boston holds an option on Sonny Gray that he can opt out of, but potentially the entire rotation is headed back for 2027. Starters 6-10 might be a concern, but for a healthy Opening Day major league roster, Breslow took care of that already.
We never actually got to see this team assembled together in 2026. Even if Curtis Mead came into the last game of the season while Garrett Crochet was on the mound, Roman was out. This year, unless there is a big trade to accommodate a move, the Hot Stove season won’t be the same. The roster is basically set. Did Breslow see the lockout as an obstacle? Maybe! He might have been thinking that teams would scramble to make moves before and after and he’d be set. For a team that was seeing it’s window open in 2025, it seems too intentional to put together the whole thing one year in with really only the Story to Arias transition as a big roster move to facilitate.
The performance of the team in 2026 was up and down, but overall we saw a number of good years from this group - Tolle, Abreu, Contreras, Rafaela, and Durbin all provide reasons to be optimistic. Roman Anthony had a good run around the hand injury. Six months off sure would be nice to let that heal. There’s reason to think 2027 can be fun. Maybe distributed a little better too.
Your Opening Day 2027 Boston Red Sox:
C: Rutschman, Wong
1: Contreras
2B: Mead, Sogard
SS: Story, Arias
3B: Durbin
OF: Roman, Rafaela, Abreau, Duran (if he’s not moved/non-tenderd), Campbell
DH: Yoshida

item.content:encoded:
When the Boston Red Sox acquired Garrett Crochet from the Chicago White Sox in December of 2024, it felt like a tale of two teams heading in very different directions. Boston had a generational crop of homegrown talent banging down to the door, headlined by Roman Anthony, Marcelo Mayer and Kristian Campbell, with Crochet as the final piece of a potential championship puzzle. As for Chicago ... well, they'd lost 100-plus games for two years in a row, and it didn't seem like that streak would end any time soon. If you were forced to bet on which team would be the first to win a playoff series, you would've put your life's savings on the Red Sox.
Turns out we all would've lost a whole bunch of money. Boston is headed home after the Wild Card Round for the second straight year, and this elimination was even more humiliating than the last. The White Sox, meanwhile, are still very much alive, sweeping the Houston Astros on the road to punch their ticket to the ALDS this weekend.
Pretty much everything we thought we knew about these teams has been flipped on its head over the last two years. How much should that change how we view the Crochet deal in hindsight? FanSided originally had the trade about even, giving the White Sox a B and the Red Sox a B- at the time. Now, though, things look a whole lot different.
White Sox' Garrett Crochet trade regrade
The Crochet return centered around three players: catcher Kyle Teel, outfielder Braden Montgomery and infielder Chase Meidroth. Teel and Montgomery were the headliners, two consensus top-100 prospects that the White Sox hoped would be the foundation for their next competitive window.
Instead, Meidroth might be the biggest win of all. He might not have the most upside, but with his contact skills and slick glove at second base, he's got an awfully high floor that should make him a big-league regular for a very long time. Meidroth posted a 115 OPS+ and 4.5 bWAR in his sophomore season, one of the biggest reasons why the White Sox are where they are right now.
But he's far from the only building block Chicago was able to acquire. Teel has had a hard time staying healthy since the trade, but when he's been on the field he's looked the part of a legit two-way catcher, solid behind the plate with elite barrel and walk rates as a hitter. If he can just avoid injury for a full season, there's no reason he can't become a top 10-15 catcher in the sport — at a minimum.
Montgomery is admittedly a bit behind the other two, a good athlete who needs to figure out how to either make more contact or pull the ball in the air more if he's going to pan out as a Major League hitter. Still: All signs point to both Meidroth and Teel becoming mainstays in Chicago's lineup for years to come, and that's a home run given the question marks around Crochet at the time — question marks that are still swirling despite the success he's had in Boston.
White Sox regrade: A
Red Sox' Garrett Crochet trade regrade
It's pretty ironic that, given the roller-coaster ride Crochet's been on across two years with the Red Sox, Boston's grade in this trade winds up pretty much right where it started.
At the time, we thought that Crochet was a high-risk, high-reward proposition, a lefty with obvious ace stuff who was dogged by workload an injury concerns. Sure enough, we've seen both sides of that coin play out so far: Crochet was one of the very best pitchers in the sport in 2025, finishing second to Tarik Skubal in AL Cy Young voting, but he managed just 30 innings of a 6.30 ERA this year before landing on the IL with a shoulder issue.
Crochet did manage to get back on the field in October, making a relief appearance in Boston's Game 2 loss on Wednesday night. And he could well have a healthy offseason and get back to making good on the six-year, $170 million extension the Red Sox gave him last March. But the fact is that he's cracked 100 innings in a season exactly twice in his baseball career; he's only cleared 150 innings once, and the very next year his shoulder started barking. Can he be a year-in, year-out ace? That remains to be seen, and that means the jury is very much still out for Boston here — especially as they struggle to find upgrades at the exact positions where Meidroth and Teel are thriving.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — For the second year in a row, the Red Sox season ended where it began: at Yankee Stadium.
On Wednesday night, before September officially turned to October, marking the true beginning of the postseason, the Red Sox were sent packing, again, by the Yankees. Unlike last year in this round, there was no need for a third game. No need for Aaron Judge. No need for Giancarlo Stanton. The Red Sox lost 9-2 on Wednesday night, a day after getting blown out 9-0 in the opener.
Instead, only embarrassment lived. Only quietness existed inside a clubhouse that will have to chew on two humiliating losses in the American League Wild Card Series.
There will be plenty from this season worth pointing to.
The Red Sox were once 14 games under .500. Then came the midsummer streak when they rattled off 15 straight wins and went 27-3 from the start of July through the beginning of August. Willson Contreras's season was vital to this club's success. Caleb Durbin's toughness and grit helped set the tone. The offense showed some malleability, deviating from its pull-side approach and becoming less one-dimensional.
All of that happened. All of it mattered.
But don't let any of it obscure the reality. Don't let the front office twist this. Don't let it off the hook too easily. The front office pivoted to Durbin only once it missed out on Alex Bregman.
And when October arrived -- pardon, the end of September -- the Red Sox finished their season with one fewer postseason win than they had a year ago.
It has now been five years since postseason baseball was last played at Fenway Park, the longest October drought for the ballpark since 1976-85.
Don't be fooled by the summer surge. Don't be fooled by the progress.
This season wasn't a success.
"Uncompetitive." Isaiah Kiner-Falefa said afterward. "We got boat-raced. To lose in the Wild Card is unacceptable."
"I mean, right now it's, regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there were quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series," manager Chad Tracy said. "And that ended for us tonight."
'I would have liked to have been trusted'
Frustration mounted in the clubhouse afterward, too. For a second straight night, Tracy pulled his starter early for Erik Miller, and it immediately backfired.
This time, it was Sonny Gray, who had allowed just one run, a solo homer to Luis García Jr. in the top of the fourth. In the fifth, Gray worked around a Trent Grisham leadoff single, recording two outs on a force out and a groundout. Yet, after a Ben Rice single put runners at first and third, Tracy inexplicably ended Gray's evening at just 70 pitches with Cody Bellinger looming.
Instantly, much like Tuesday night, the Yankees capitalized. Bellinger laced a single to right, extending the lead to 2-0.
Forced to piece together the rest of the game with a bullpen that included appearances from Garrett Crochet and Garrett Whitlock, the Red Sox watched the Yankees pour on eight runs against their relievers.
A disgruntled Gray didn't hold back his sentiments following the outing.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League the third time through the order," Gray said. He then paused for a moment. "I think that's a fact. I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment."
Gray was spot-on. He, indeed, was the best starter in the American League the third time through the order, carrying a 1.99 ERA in 45 ⅓ innings pitched, a large enough sample size.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that are telling you what to do, because this is baseball and the data is here to help us," Contreras said. "But at the end of the day, we're going to need experienced and veteran guys to win games."
That points to a larger issue that has followed lead executive Craig Breslow.
The April firing of manager Alex Cora and his staff might have been the right decision. Tracy (who was named the full-time skipper last week), ideally, is the manager that Breslow envisioned at the helm. But don't let their torrid summer misconstrue the split in the clubhouse. Some players remain convinced the new coaching staff had little to do with their success.
That might have been Gray's last time in a Red Sox uniform -- or in any uniform, as the 36-year-old has contemplated retirement. Asked if he would want to return next season to the Red Sox if he decided to play:
"I don't know," Gray responded.
Roster questions looming
Roman Anthony needs to prove he can stay healthy. He was pulled from Game 1 after re-aggravating the same right hand that kept him out for 101 games. Anthony went for an MRI in Boston early Wednesday morning before returning that afternoon. It's still unclear if he needs surgery.
"After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%, kind of as you would expect," he said. "But I think for me, it was to a point where it was tolerable, and I was taking certain swings that were sketchy but was still able to come back and recover enough to just be in there every single day. But ultimately, I just took a few swings here recently where that wasn't the case."
Remember the Big Three? Anthony, Kristian Campbell and Marcelo Mayer were supposed to represent the next wave of the Red Sox.
What do the Red Sox do with Campbell, who was stuck in Triple-A all season and put up subpar numbers? Mayer was supposed to be the heir apparent to Trevor Story. He was traded to San Francisco.
Surely, Story has aged out of being an everyday shortstop.
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela and right fielder Wilyer Abreu are proven everyday players. But if Anthony isn't healthy, the Red Sox will need to patch up left field. Jarren Duran might have played his last season in a Red Sox uniform, with many suspecting he will be traded in the offseason.
And, despite the offense coming alive this summer, that could be viewed as fool's gold. During their 37-game surge, the Sox hit .258 with a .445 slugging percentage and their run creation was 15% better than league average. Over their final 47 games, those numbers fell to a .236 average, .382 slugging percentage and they created runs 6% below the league-average mark.
Their late-season woes looked much more like the offense from the first 78 games, when the club hit .244 with a .385 slugging percentage, than the one that transformed its season.
"Obviously disappointed," Story said on getting bounced from the postseason. "A lot of thoughts, but proud of this group, proud of this team. With all the hate and everything going around, the way this team came together, we really turned the season around to get back into this position. It was something that was special."
The summer run was special, yes.
But don't let this club off the hook.
The season wasn't a success.

item.content:encoded:
Worcester: Cancelled (rain), end of season
Remember when Portland’s last game of the season was cancelled due to rain? Oh, that was just last week.
Well, as we’re stuck in a cycle of weekend storms, the last game of the season was cancelled for the WooSox. A factor in this decision was Worcester being eliminated from playoff contention on Saturday night. Still, for the season to end so unceremoniously calls for at least some commemoration, and so I’d like to shout out some names on the roster. I originally intended on going down the line on the website and speculate on future contributions to the team, but, by my estimation, especially since the trade for Adley Rutschman that had a ripple effect through the organization, a good portion of Worcester’s roster are either one-year placeholders until the farm gets replenished with the next couple of drafts or guys that are dealing with significant injuries. So, here’s to the guys that may not be that:
Allan Castro finished the season with 77 RBIs, two behind Bobby Dalbec for the team record since they relocated to Worcester five years ago… and saying that relocation happened six seasons ago is crazy for someone who went to the first home stand under pandemic crowd protocols. Castro really was a constant for the offense amidst a handful of platoon guys cycling through the team and that can’t be understated. He batted doubtful games back into contention and sealed close games away. If I pick a workhorse/general player of the year, it’s him or Braiden Ward, but only because Franklin Arias started the year in Portland.
Speaking of Braiden Ward, I personally was sad to see Brennan Bernardino go this offseason but loved the return from Colorado. And he performed fantastically, particularly near the end of the season. He ended up swiping 61 total bags and ther’s some clamor around a potential call-up to the Sox who, despite being a generally quick team in terms of baserunning, lack a real Dave Roberts-esque “when you see him, you know he’s going to steal” threat. Ward provides that, is defensively versatile, playing second as well as center field, and is pretty reliable with the bat in a pinch.
Franklin Arias is banging on the door and he will definitively be getting the call either in 2027 or Opening Day 2028, depending entirely on the length of the lockout. Either way, though, keeping him off the 40-man roster for now means, even with a lockout, he’ll get valuable time to improve his exceptional swing even more, though not against Major League arms. His totals across Portland and Worcester read like an All-Star caliber player: 28 home runs, .323/.400/.557 slash line, a 14% strikeout rate, and a plus glove in the infield to boot. Arias may or may not live up to his sky high prospect status, but pencil him in to the next iteration of this Red Sox team, whenever that comes.
John Holobetz will also likely be given the call in 2027. He’s still just 24. The 6’3” righty struck out 132 in 119 innings, walked just 36, had a WIP of a hair under 1.25, but even more comforting is he outperformed his Portland numbers in Worcester, signaling quick growth. While it’s sad that Quinn Priester missed 2026 with an injury, he was a world-beater in 2025, and the value of having steady presence in the rotation can’t be understated Depending how he bounces back in 2027, especially with the Brewers emerging as an NL front runner, expect that trade to go down in the history books as a win-win.
Hayden Mullins also put in his best work in 2026, and more specifically, directly before his promotion to Triple-A right before the end of the season. He celebrated his 26th birthday last Monday and so, in his age-25 season, Mullins was exactly what Portland needed in a rotation guy, especially following Anthony Eyannson’s departure. He struck out 132 in 92 innings, walked 49, lacked the longevity that Holobetz and others in the rotation had but did not give up long balls, getting taken yard just seven times all season (and even one of those was in his only Worcester appearance.) The 6’0” lefty will continue his development in 2027 before likely a late season call-up; it’s possible the team explores some multi-inning reliever roles depending on how this development goes.
Of course, too, the team’s former first-round draft pick Mikey Romero and current millionaire Kristian Campbell are still kicking around Wrocester, and the latter wants a redemption arc after a rough 2025. Neither saw any Major League time due to a cluttered roster and a multitude of other reasons, but don’t count either out for a platoon role next year, pending a lengthy lockout. You want guys looking better in September than they did in April, and while Campbell swung somewhat of a hot bat in the spring, I think that notion is true for both of these guys. The same is even true with Jedixson Paez (who saw Major League action, but don’t mention this to him) Blake Wehunt and Gage Ziehl. These are all guys to watch in 2027, provided some trade for a hole on the roster doesn’t call for dealing one of them (I think Campbell is pretty set on this roster given his price tag.) But, depth is a good problem to have.
And so ends my fourth full season providing Minor Lines for Over The Monster. You’ll see me kicking around during the playoff push and the offseason providing input on pieces that can make this 2027 team - and farm - even better than the 2026 version. Thanks so much for reading all season, and Go Sox!

item.content:encoded:
Kristian Campbell reflects on a rollercoaster 2026 season with WooSox
WORCESTER — Seated inside the Worcester Red Sox dugout Thursday afternoon, Kristian Campbell took stock of his 2026 season — while taking a break from the gray boot that’s occupied his left foot for the past few days.
“It’s been pretty solid,” the soft-spoken Campbell told the T&G. “I mean, I learned a lot about myself.”
A week prior, the 24-year-old outfielder landed on the 7-day injured list with a broken left toe, which effectively ended his AAA season.
“He was a big part of what we’ve been doing,” WooSox acting manager Iggy Suarez said. “So, it’s definitely a downer for that.”
Path less traveled
As Campbell comes into Polar Park each day, the Worcester Red Sox player takes a unique route to the home clubhouse.
He enters through the parking lot located beyond the left-field wall, strolls through the blue seats in the stands, touches the warning track dirt for a few steps before walking down the stairs of the home dugout. It’s not a path many (if any) players take when arriving at the ballpark.
But like his journey inside the Red Sox organization for the past three seasons, Campbell’s taken the path less traveled. From High A to Triple A in 2024, to the big leagues and back to the minors last year, to spending his entire 2026 season in Triple A, it’s been an interesting course for the 6-foot-3, 210-pound Campbell.
“Everybody has their own journey,” Campbell told the T&G last year.
In the spring of 2025, Campbell impressed the Red Sox brass enough to garner a spot on Boston’s Opening Day roster and shortly after that he inked an eight-year, $60 million contract extension.
“It was the first time, I guess, that playing hard and just playing for the love of the game actually, literally, paid off,” Campbell said last season.
Boston saw dividends right away from calling up Campbell — and giving him a contract extension. He was named the American League Rookie of the Month for April after batting .301 with 4 home runs, 12 RBIs and a .902 OPS through his first 29 big-league games.
But then the struggles started for the then Red Sox rookie last year — at the plate (where he hit in every spot except leadoff and No. 2) and in the field (2B, CF, LF and DH). Starting on May 1, Campbell went into a prolonged slump in which he hit .159 with 2 homers, 9 RBIs and a .465 OPS across a 38-game stretch.
On June 20, 2025, Campbell was demoted to Triple-A Worcester. Nearly 15 months later, Campbell remains in AAA.
“In the moment, we certainly thought Kristian was ready and felt like he was going to hit the ground running and he did,” Red Sox senior director of player development Brian Abraham told the T&G this week. “But then, as the league had a better feel for him and found out his weaknesses, it was a little bit harder for him to adjust in the moment.
“So, I think it’s just a reminder that it’s really hard to not only have success, but to fail, then have success again,” Abraham added. “And making sure that we’re supporting him as much as we can (in) the day-to-day, making sure that the highs aren’t too high and the lows aren’t too low.”
Sticking to the plan
Although Campbell started slow to start his 2026 season, the right-handed hitter — with an athletic yet unorthodox swing — found his footing at the plate.
In July, Campbell hit .379 (22 for 58) with 2 HR and 11 RBIs.
“We’re starting to see him believing in himself again,” Suarez said at the time.
“To be able to work through some of the adversity and the struggles — (and) to get to a point this last couple of months where he was performing well, was, really cool to see,” Abraham said.
Through five games this month, Campbell was hitting .412 (7 for 17) with 1 HR, 5 RBIs and 4 walks. He saw the ball well and sprayed the ball all over the field — shades of his 2024 and early 2025 self.
“I think we were looking at someone who could’ve been in the mix for a potential call-up,” Abraham said. “But, obviously, that’s not in the cards anymore.”
During his third at-bat in a game against the Lehigh Valley IronPigs on Sept. 8, Campbell hit his foot with his bat on a follow-through from his swing. The result: a broken left toe.
He was placed on the 7-day IL two days later.
“It’s unfortunate,” Suarez said.
“It’s just part of baseball. Things happen,” Campbell said. “I just got to make sure I treat myself the right way and make sure this injury doesn't prolong. So, I’ll be good, sooner than later.”
Across 109 games and 371 at-bats, Campbell collected a .256 batting average with 8 HRs and 51 RBIs. His 2026 season was another case of Dr. Jekyll (second half) and Mr. Hyde (first half).
“(In the) first half (I was) trying stuff,” Campbell said. “(In the) second half (I was) sticking to (my) plan. That’s pretty much it, and that tells you two different things you get when you stick to your plan versus trying stuff. That’s how I think about it. And now I know exactly what makes me that type of player, so I’m going to stick to that.”
Back on the map
While Campbell has been sidelined this week in Worcester and the AAA club wraps up its regular season on Sunday, he continues to stick around and work out each day at Polar Park.
Campbell hopes to heal in time and stay ready as part of a Red Sox taxi squad in Fort Myers, Florida in case the Red Sox need reinforcements during the playoffs.
While a late season/postseason call up seems like a long shot at this point for Campbell, the former top Red Sox prospect has positioned himself to be in the conversation for another crack at Boston’s Opening Day roster in 2027.
“I think the guy we saw the last two months can compete with a lot of players in the big leagues to be a competitive and impactful player day in and day out in the lineup,” Abraham said. “So, obviously the work that he put in this year and the consistency needs to carry over into spring training, but I think he’s put himself in a position where he’s certainly back in those conversations, back on the map.
“And again, I don't think he was ever off (it), but to see the performance happen in real time in Worcester, not only just the hits and getting on base, but the actual under the radar, under the hood information that we value as well, were all trending up. So, definitely someone who’s going to be in those conversations as we head to spring next year.”
This year was another learning curve for Campbell. His baseball journey has been anything but linear over the past three years.
And as Campbell took stock of his 2026 season, the 24-year-old outfielder concluded with one final thought on his future.
“To be a Major League baseball player,” Campbell said. “I took this year to develop. But the future, it’s funny, I actually was thinking about that. More the mental side stuff for me. I like to focus on one day at a time. I don’t really think too much into the future, but obviously being a baseball player and knowing what I want to do, I do obviously want to be a Major League baseball player.
“I’m at the highest level and I’m going to keep working towards that. So, whenever I get the opportunity to do it, I’ll be ready.”
—Contact Tommy Cassell at tcassell@telegram.com. Follow him on X, formerly known as Twitter, @TommyCassell_.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox could have a slew of pitching reinforcements returning before the playoffs begin, including Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, and maybe even Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Justin Slaten will not be among them.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on September 15 told reporters (including Tim Healey of The Boston Globe) that Slaten got a PRP injection in his arm to address a flexor issue. His season is over after multiple attempts to ramp up for a rehab assignment and eventual return.
Slaten has been quite injury prone over his three years with the Red Sox. He went on the injured list for the first time this season in early April and didn't return until mid-May. For the second straight year, he'll finish his season with less than 35 innings pitched.
Justin Slaten's season with Red Sox ends after he gets PCP injection for flexor injury
The righty has dabbled in the extremes this season, finishing with a 4.60 ERA over 31.1 innings. In June, Slaten's worst month this year, he allowed nine runs on 17 hits over 11 outings. July was his best, during which he let up just one run on five hits over nine appearances. His WHIP has starkly increased over the past year, from 1.09 in 2025 to 1.37.
When the Red Sox can get Slaten's best, he's one of the biggest threats out of their bullpen. But he's often injured or prone to blowups that keep him from showing the best he can offer. It will be interesting to see his role next season when Boston has more healthy pitching depth it could push to the bullpen.
Red Sox confirm Kristian Campbell's season is over due to foot injury, ending breakout
Kristian Campbell's season has also ended prematurely due to an injury. The outfielder will be out for the rest of the year due to a left foot contusion, according to Tommy Cassell of the Worcester Telegram & Gazette.
The WooSox pulled Campbell from their September 8 game due to the injury. Even before the announcement of his IL stint, it was evident that Campbell's season could be over, as Worcester's last regular season game is on Septembet 20.
Campbell's injury ends a resurgent second half for the 24 year old. He slashed .311/.430/.497 over 51 games after the All-Star break and, had he been healthy, he might've been selected to come up and help the major league team while Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White are injured.
Romy Gonzalez continues tear following arm injury scare with WooSox
On the same day Campbell was pulled from the WooSox's lineup, Romy Gonzalez was, too. An arm injury led to a week on the shelf for the utility infielder, but he joined the Triple-A lineup again on September 15.
Gonzalez has resumed the tear he was on before his arm flared up. He logged two hits, including a double, in his return and boosted his September slash line to .500/.520/.727 over six games. Gonzalez has hit so well lately that it could be time to call him back up to the major leagues to give Boston's slumping offense a boost.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox got some bad news on Tuesday. Top prospect Kristian Campbell is going on the IL, which means his season is over.
Campbell was with the Worcester Red Sox at the Triple-A level. There, he suffered a foot contusion, per Tommy Cassell.
In 109 games with the WooSox, Campbell has a .256 average this season with a .763 OPS. That's with 8 home runs, 51 RBIs, and 73 walks. Defensively, he's spent most of his time in the outfield. That's despite largely playing second base in 2025.
Notably, Campbell was showing improvement in the second half. In 36 games since the All-Star break, he was hitting .333 with a 1.009 OPS, to go along with 6 home runs. That had, seemingly, made him an option to come up to the majors.
Kristian Campbell Didn't Play for the Boston Red Sox in 2026
In 2025, Kristian Campbell made the Boston Red Sox roster coming out of Spring Training. He was the Opening Day second baseman, and there was a lot of excitement about what he could end up being.
Things didn't work out. In 67 games, he hit .223 with a .664 OPS. Campbell had 6 home runs and 21 RBIs. To go along with those offensive struggles, he was a bit of a liability defensively at second base. So, the Red Sox would often play him in the outfield, but they already have a logjam of players there.
Eventually, Campbell was sent to Triple-A to work on improving his swing and to find a defensive position. That's where he'd spend the entire season.
"Overall pleased, minus the injury," Red Sox senior director of player development Brian Abraham said. "I think we were looking at someone who could've been in the mix for a potential call-up. But, obviously, that's not in the cards anymore."
At the MLB level, the Red Sox have had some injury issues. That's forced them, at times, to lean on players who would normally be bench players or borderline players between Triple-A and the majors. However, they resisted rushing Campbell back to Boston, after seemingly rushing him in 2025. With his improving bat as of late, there was some excitement that he could be returning to the majors soon, but that's not going to happen now.
The Future for the Red Sox and Campbell
While it may seem strange for Campbell to be away from the MLB team for so long, his future with the Red Sox is still bright.
Campbell is finishing up his age 24 season. He's still relatively young and when he does get his next chance with the Red Sox, he'll better know what to expect at the MLB level, and he'll be going to that level with more development under his belt.
The Red Sox and Campbell are also committed to one another. In April of 2025, the Red Sox signed Campbell to an eight-year, $60 million contract. So, he's going to be with Boston for the foreseeable future, regardless of the upcoming CBA changes.
The challenge now for Boston is to find what position Campbell will play when he rejoins the MLB team. There's still a logjam in the outfield. Campbell still isn't viewed as a great option defensively, and those infield spots are filling quickly. So, will a move be made to clear space for Campbell?

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox fans will not be seeing former top prospect Kristian Campbell in the big leagues at all this season, unfortunately.
On Tuesday, Tommy Cassell of the Worcester T&G Sports reported that Campbell's season is over. Campbell was placed on the seven-day Injured List due to a left foot contusion on Sep. 10. Cassell reported that Campbell will not be able to return before Triple-A Worcester's season ends on Sep. 20.
"Some injury updates today in AAA Worcester: Tanner Houck is scheduled to pitch one inning (20-25 pitches) in relief," Cassell wrote. "Romy Gonzalez is in at DH despite being a bit banged up. Iggy Suarez mentioned he's "an option" to contribute with the Red Sox moving forward. Kristian Campbell is out for the rest of the WooSox season. 'He was a big part of what we've been doing,' Suarez said. 'So, it's definitely a downer for that.'"
Kristian Campbell Is Done For The Year
That's some really unfortunate news for one of the most intriguing players in the Red Sox's system. Campbell made the big league club out of Spring Training in 2025 as the first member of the "Big 3," including him, Roman Anthony and Marcelo Mayer. He was red-hot out of the gate to the point that Boston handed him an eight-year, $60 million deal. But things took a turn afterward. Campbell was demoted to Triple-A in June, 2025. He hasn't been in the majors since.
Campbell played in 73 down in Triple-A last season and then didn't make the Red Sox's big league club out of camp. He has been down in the minors all season this year trying to work his way back.
The 24-year-old spent the season in the outfield as Boston tried to slow things down after moving him around all over the place last year. For Boston, it is loaded in the outfield to the point that there was a logjam early on in the season. Then, despite the Red Sox losing Roman Anthony to the Injured List for a while, there still wasn't space for Campbell in the majors.
Overall, Campbell wrapped up his season after playing in 109 games for Triple-A and slashing .256/.383/.380 with a .763 OPS, eight homers and 51 RBIs. Hopefully, he's able to get back on track and get back into the mix by the time Spring Training rolls around. Who could've seen this coming back in 2025? Campbell looked like a franchise cornerstone piece. Unfortunately, he hasn't been in the majors in over a year and now that won't be happening this year.
